sections.title: The Dawn of Mathematics: The Human Need to Count
The Revolution of Śhūnya: When Nothing Became Something
Filling the Spaces: Fractions and Rational Numbers
Real Numbers: Decimals and Cyclic Patterns

slides.title: Counting came first
slides.kicker: Mathematics was born in the dirt, not classrooms
bullets: Long before cities, laws or the study of stars, humanity had a fundamental practical necessity: the need to keep count.
Mathematics did not begin in a classroom with equations on a board; it began in the dirt, on the bark of trees, and on bones.
Counting was survival: early herders and farmers needed to track what they had and what was missing.
slides.note: Before any book, math lived on bones and dirt!

slides.title: Pebbles counted cows
slides.kicker: One pebble, one cow: the first numbers
bullets: Picture a small settlement on the banks of the Saraswati river, its cattle going out to graze each morning.
The herder placed one pebble in a clay pot for every cow that left, and removed one pebble for every cow that returned.
An empty pot at dusk meant the herd was safe; pebbles remaining meant cows were missing.
This matching of one object to another is one-to-one correspondence, the birth of the Natural Numbers N = {1, 2, 3, 4, ...}.
slides.note: Ek pebble, ek cow. Simple and perfect.

slides.title: The Lebombo bone
slides.kicker: A 35,000-year-old lunar calendar
bullets: The earliest physical evidence of recording natural numbers comes from Africa, as tally marks carved into bone.
The Lebombo Bone, from the Lebombo Mountains between South Africa and Swaziland, dates back about 35,000 years.
It carries 29 distinct, deliberately carved, uniformly sized notches.
Anthropologists believe it was a lunar phase counter or a menstrual calendar: early humans tracking time through natural numbers.
slides.note: The first mathematicians wrote on bone.

slides.title: The Ishango bone
slides.kicker: Primes and doubling, 20,000 years ago
bullets: The Ishango bone was found near the headwaters of the Nile in the Democratic Republic of Congo, dating to around 20,000 BCE.
It holds three columns of asymmetrical notches, grouped with clear mathematical intent.
One column groups notches into 11, 13, 17 and 19, the prime numbers between 10 and 20.
Another column seems to demonstrate multiplication by 2, the idea of doubling.

slides.title: The line began at one
slides.kicker: For millennia, nothing had no number
bullets: For millennia the number line started at 1; give away five apples and no number described your state.
You simply had a void, a lack of apples, not a number.
Civilisations like the Babylonians and Mayans used placeholders, symbols marking an empty column in a written number.
But they never treated nothing as a number you could add, subtract and multiply.

slides.title: Śhūnyatā: philosophy first
slides.kicker: Meditation emptied the mind into mathematics
bullets: In the Upanishads and Buddhist literature, well before the 7th century BCE, Śhūnyatā meant emptiness or nothingness.
Śhūnya means zero; śhūnyatā meant emptying the mind of vṛttis, its fluctuations, to reach perfect stillness.
Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, around the 3rd century BCE, describe śhūnyatā leading to control over mind, body and senses.
Because Indian thinkers revered emptiness, they could welcome nothingness first in philosophy, then in mathematics.

slides.title: From bindu to number
slides.kicker: A dot gains rules and becomes zero
bullets: In the Bakhśhālī Manuscript, dated to the early centuries CE, a bold dot, the bindu, represents zero.
A symbol is just a mark on a page until it has rules.
In the Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta of 628 CE, Brahmagupta explicitly defined zero as a number with rules for its use.
That turned śhūnya into a fully operational number and transformed mathematics.

slides.title: Placeholder is not zero
slides.kicker: Empty column marker versus a true number
bullets: Babylonian and Mayan placeholder symbols only showed that a column in a written number was empty.
A placeholder cannot be added, subtracted or multiplied, because it is not a number.
Brahmagupta's leap was to transform the void itself into a number with arithmetic rules.
This monumental leap of 628 CE was inspired by Indian philosophical traditions.

slides.title: Dhana and Ṛiṇa
slides.kicker: Commerce gave the world negative numbers
bullets: Brahmagupta asked: if 5 – 5 = 0, what happens when we subtract a larger number from a smaller one, like 3 – 5?
He grounded his answer in the reality of commerce and life.
Fortunes (Dhana) are positive numbers, representing wealth or assets.
Debts (Ṛiṇa) are negative numbers, representing what you owe.

slides.title: Left of zero
slides.kicker: Negatives complete the set of integers
bullets: By moving to the left of zero on the number line, Brahmagupta formally introduced negative numbers.
Positive natural numbers, their negative counterparts and zero together create the set of Integers.
The set is denoted Z, from the German word Zahlen, meaning numbers.
On the line, debts stretch left from Śhūnya and fortunes stretch right.

slides.title: Brahmagupta's addition rules
slides.kicker: Written 1,300 years ago, used today
bullets: A fortune plus a fortune is a fortune: 5 + 4 = 9.
A debt plus a debt is a debt: (–5) + (–4) = –9; if you owe 5 and borrow 4 more, you owe 9.
A fortune minus zero is a fortune, and a debt minus zero is a debt: 7 – 0 = 7 and –6 – 0 = –6.
We still use these rules exactly as Brahmagupta wrote them over 1,300 years ago.

slides.title: Minus times minus
slides.kicker: Removing debts makes you richer
bullets: The product of a debt and a fortune is a debt: (–3) × 4 = –12, four debts of 3 totalling 12 owed.
The product of two debts is a fortune: (–3) × (–4) = 12.
Multiplying by a negative number represents the removal of that debt.
If someone takes away four of your debts worth 3 each, you are effectively 12 richer, so (–3) × (–4) = +12.

slides.title: Counting to measuring
slides.kicker: Fields divided, ghee measured
bullets: As society grew more complex, measuring became just as important as counting.
If a farmer divides a field of wheat among his three children, how much does each child get?
If a recipe calls for half a cup of ghee, we need a number for a part of a whole.
Numbers that represent parts of a whole are called fractions.

slides.title: Negative fractions
slides.kicker: Every fraction has an opposite
bullets: Just as 3 has –3 and 19 has –19, every positive fraction has an additive inverse.
The inverse of 3/4 is –3/4 and the inverse of 19/7 is –19/7; these are negative fractions.
The minus sign can sit in front, on the numerator, or on the denominator: –1/5 = (–1)/5 = 1/(–5).
All three forms name exactly the same number.

slides.title: Rational numbers Q
slides.kicker: Integers and fractions, one family
bullets: Combining all integers with all fractions, positive and negative, gives the Rational Numbers, denoted Q for quotient.
A rational number is any number that can be expressed as p/q, where p and q are integers and q is not 0.
Whole numbers qualify too: 5 = 5/1 and –10 = –10/1, so Q includes the naturals, wholes and integers.
Q is for quotient, the result of one integer divided by another.

slides.title: One number, many names
slides.kicker: Equivalent fractions, one standard form
bullets: Rational numbers have no unique representation: –3/1 = –6/2 = –9/3 = –30/10 = –6078/2026.
These are equivalent rational numbers, or equivalent fractions.
We may divide a common factor out of the numerator and denominator: 12/30 becomes 2/5 by dividing both by 6.
By agreement, p/q on the number line has q not 0 and p, q co-prime, sharing no factor other than 1.

slides.title: A crisis of lengths
slides.kicker: When lengths refused to be fractions
bullets: For centuries, mathematicians believed every measurable length in the universe could be a ratio of two integers.
Around 800 BCE, Baudhāyana composed the Śhulbasūtra, a manual for constructing complex geometric fire altars.
In his exact constructions he quickly encountered lengths that defied fractions.
The ancient Greeks encountered the same crisis a few centuries later.

slides.title: The unit square diagonal
slides.kicker: Baudhāyana–Pythagoras reveals sqrt(2)
bullets: Take a square whose each side is exactly 1 unit long.
By the Baudhāyana–Pythagoras Theorem, the diagonal d satisfies 1^2 + 1^2 = d^2.
So d^2 = 2, and the length of the diagonal is sqrt(2).
Numbers on the number line that cannot be expressed as a ratio of integers are called Irrational Numbers.

slides.title: Proof by contradiction
slides.kicker: Hippasus assumes the opposite, c. 400 BCE
bullets: The first proof of the irrationality of sqrt(2) is due to Hippasus, a member of the Pythagorean school around 400 BCE.
His technique is Proof by Contradiction: assume the opposite of what you want to prove.
Then show that this assumption leads to a logical disaster.
Assume sqrt(2) = p/q in its simplest form, with p and q co-prime integers and q not 0.

items: p and q both turn even

slides.title: The disaster unfolds
slides.kicker: Both even contradicts co-prime
bullets: Squaring and multiplying gives 2q^2 = p^2, so p^2 is even, and a number with an even square must itself be even.
Write p = 2k; then 2q^2 = 4k^2, so q^2 = 2k^2, and q must be even too.
Now p and q share a common factor 2, though Step 1 declared them co-prime.
The assumption destroys itself, so no fraction p/q can equal sqrt(2).

slides.title: The unbroken line R
slides.kicker: Rationals plus irrationals, no gaps left
bullets: When we unite the dense web of Rational Numbers with the unfillable gaps of Irrational Numbers, we get the Real Numbers R.
The real line is unbroken and continuous.
The easiest way to distinguish a rational number from an irrational number is to look at its decimal expansion.

slides.title: Two fates of a decimal
slides.kicker: Terminate or repeat, nothing else
bullets: Divide the numerator of a rational number by its denominator: exactly one of two things will happen.
It terminates: the division eventually leaves remainder 0 and the decimal stops, like 3/8 = 0.375.
It repeats: the remainder never becomes 0 and the digits loop infinitely, like 5/11 = 0.454545... = 0.45 with a bar on 45.
There is no third possibility for a rational number.

slides.title: Why decimals repeat
slides.kicker: Six remainders, then the loop
bullets: Imagine calculating 1/7 by long division: dividing by 7, each remainder can only be 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6.
Remainder 0 would end the division, so it never appears while the decimal keeps going.
There are only finitely many possible remainders, so some remainder must show up a second time.
Once a remainder repeats, the entire division process loops, creating a repeating decimal.

slides.title: Predict the decimal type
slides.kicker: Prime factors of the denominator decide
bullets: We can predict terminating or repeating without doing the long division, using the prime factors of the denominator.
Take 3/20 in lowest terms: 20 = 2^2 × 5, so only 2s and 5s appear.
Multiply numerator and denominator by 5 to get 15/100 = 0.15, a terminating decimal.
The expansion terminates precisely when the prime factors of q are only 2, only 5, or both; then q becomes a power of 10.

flashcards.back: Matching one object to exactly one other object, like one pebble per cow in a pot; it was the birth of the Natural Numbers.

flashcards.back: N = {1, 2, 3, 4, ...}, born from the basic human need to keep count.

quiz.q: According to the book, where did mathematics begin?
options: In the dirt, on the bark of trees and on bones
In a classroom with equations on a board
On paper scrolls in royal courts
quiz.why: Before cities and laws, the practical need to keep count started math in the dirt, on bark and on bones.

quiz.q: In the Saraswati settlement story, what did the herder place in a clay pot for every cow that left?
options: A notch carved on a bone
quiz.why: One pebble went in per cow leaving; one came out per cow returning, until the pot was empty.

quiz.q: What do anthropologists believe the 29 notches of the Lebombo bone were used for?
options: A lunar phase counter or menstrual calendar
quiz.why: The 35,000-year-old bone's 29 uniform notches show early humans tracking time through natural numbers.

quiz.q: One Ishango bone column groups notches into 11, 13, 17 and 19. Why is this grouping a mathematical marvel?
options: They are the even numbers between 10 and 20
They are the first four perfect squares
They are the prime numbers between 10 and 20
quiz.why: The book highlights this column as the primes between 10 and 20; another column shows doubling.

quiz.q: For millennia, where did the number line start?
quiz.why: Nothing had no number yet; the line began at 1 until Brahmagupta transformed the void into zero.

quiz.q: The bold dot (bindu) representing zero appears in which manuscript?
quiz.why: The Bakhśhālī Manuscript, early centuries CE, shows the transition from blank space to a bold dot.

quiz.q: What made Brahmagupta's zero different from the Babylonian and Mayan placeholder?
options: His was a dot, theirs a circle
His zero was a full number with arithmetic rules, theirs only marked an empty column
His zero held larger place values
Theirs could be multiplied but not added
quiz.why: Placeholders only marked an empty column; Brahmagupta made nothing a number you can add, subtract and multiply.

quiz.q: Which chain describes how zeroness entered mathematics, as the book tells it?
options: Greek philosophy to Babylonian tablets to India
Upanishads and Buddhist thought, then Āryabhaṭa, finally Brahmagupta
Patanjali's Yoga Sutras directly into commerce
Mayan placeholders copied by Indian traders
quiz.why: Śhūnyatā from philosophy flowed through Āryabhaṭa and finally into Brahmagupta's rules of 628 CE.

quiz.q: In Brahmagupta's language of numbers, what does Ṛiṇa stand for?
quiz.why: Debts (Ṛiṇa) are negative numbers, while fortunes (Dhana) are positive numbers of wealth.

quiz.q: Calculate (–5) + (–4) using Brahmagupta's rules.
quiz.why: A debt plus a debt is a debt: owing 5 and borrowing 4 more means 9 owed, so –9.

quiz.q: In high-altitude Ladakh it is 4 °C at noon; by midnight the temperature drops by 15 °C. What is the midnight temperature?
quiz.why: 4 – 15 = –11; a drop by 15 moves you 15 steps to the left of 4 on the number line.

quiz.q: Using the book's debt picture, why does (–3) × (–4) give +12?
options: Because –3 and –4 cancel to zero and then regrow
Because multiplying by a negative removes the four debts of 3, leaving you 12 richer
Because debts double each time they multiply
Because a fortune of 4 times a debt of 3 turns positive
quiz.why: A negative multiplier is removal: taking away four debts worth 3 each effectively adds 12.

quiz.q: Why is the set of rational numbers called Q?
quiz.why: Q stands for quotient, since a rational number is one integer divided by another.

quiz.q: What is the additive inverse of 3/4?
quiz.why: Every positive fraction has an additive inverse; just as 3 has –3, the fraction 3/4 has –3/4.

quiz.q: Reduce 12/30 to its lowest terms as the book does.
quiz.why: Divide both numerator and denominator by their common factor 6 to reach 2/5.

quiz.q: Which chain of equivalent rational numbers matches the book exactly?
quiz.why: The book lists –3/1 = –6/2 = –9/3 = –30/10 = –6078/2026 as equivalent rational numbers.

quiz.q: What is the Śhulbasūtra, composed by Baudhāyana around 800 BCE?
options: A manual for constructing complex geometric fire altars
A book of arithmetic tables for traders
A commentary on the Yoga Sutras
quiz.why: The Śhulbasūtra guided altar construction, where Baudhāyana met lengths that defied fractions.

quiz.q: A number on the number line that cannot be expressed as a ratio of integers is called?
quiz.why: Irrational numbers are exactly those lengths that no fraction p/q can name.

quiz.q: In the proof, why does 2q^2 = p^2 force p to be even?
options: Because p is co-prime with q
Because p^2 is 2 times an integer, so p^2 is even, and a number with an even square is even
Because squaring always makes numbers even
quiz.why: p^2 equals 2 times the integer q^2, so p^2 is even; if a square is even, the number itself is even.

quiz.q: Where exactly does the contradiction strike in Hippasus' proof of sqrt(2)?
options: p turns out to be odd instead of even
q turns out to be zero
Both p and q turn out even, sharing factor 2, though they were assumed co-prime
Squaring a fraction is not allowed
quiz.why: Deducing p even and q even breaks the simplest-form promise that p and q share no factor but 1.

quiz.q: What is 3/8 written as a decimal?
quiz.why: Dividing 3 by 8 eventually leaves remainder 0, giving the terminating decimal 0.375.

quiz.q: How does 5/11 behave as a decimal?
quiz.why: The remainder never becomes 0, so the digits 4 and 5 loop infinitely: 5/11 = 0.454545...

quiz.q: Which of these fractions has a terminating decimal expansion?
quiz.why: 20 = 2^2 × 5 has only 2s and 5s as prime factors, so the decimal terminates at 0.15.

quiz.q: Why do only 2s and 5s in the denominator guarantee a terminating decimal?
options: Because they are the smallest primes, so division ends quickly
Because multiplying by suitable factors turns such a denominator into a power of 10
Because such fractions are always smaller than 1
quiz.why: 10 = 2 × 5, so a denominator of only 2s and 5s scales to 10, 100, 1000; 20 became 100.

examples.title: The pebble pot audit
examples.problem: A herder on the banks of the Saraswati places one pebble in a clay pot for every cow that leaves in the morning, and removes one pebble for every cow that returns in the evening. He placed 9 pebbles at dawn and has removed 8 by dusk, with 1 pebble still in the pot. How many cows are missing, and how does one-to-one correspondence tell him?
steps: Morning: 9 cows leave, so the pot holds 9 pebbles, one per cow.
Evening: each returning cow removes exactly one pebble, so 8 pebbles removed means 8 cows returned.
One pebble remains, so one cow that left has not yet returned.
The leftover pebble is the unmatched object in the one-to-one match, and it points straight at the missing cow.
examples.answer: 1 cow is missing; the single leftover pebble is its unmatched partner.

examples.title: The spice trader's ledger
examples.problem: A spice trader takes a loan (debt) of Rs 850. The next day he makes a profit (fortune) of Rs 1,200. The following week he incurs a loss of Rs 450. Write this sequence as an equation using integers and calculate his final financial standing.
steps: Represent the loan as a debt (Ṛiṇa): –850.
Represent the profit as a fortune (Dhana): +1200.
Represent the loss as a debt: –450.
Write the equation: –850 + 1200 – 450.
First combine the fortune and the loan: –850 + 1200 = +350.
Then apply the loss: +350 – 450 = –100.
examples.answer: –850 + 1200 – 450 = –100, so his final standing is a debt (Ṛiṇa) of Rs 100.

examples.title: Why sqrt(2) is irrational
examples.problem: Prove that sqrt(2) is irrational, following Hippasus' Proof by Contradiction.
steps: Assume the opposite: sqrt(2) = p/q in its simplest form, where p and q are co-prime integers and q is not 0.
Square both sides: 2 = p^2/q^2.
Multiply both sides by q^2: 2q^2 = p^2.
p^2 equals 2 times the integer q^2, so p^2 is even; if the square is even, the number itself is even, so p = 2k for some integer k.
Substitute p = 2k: 2q^2 = (2k)^2 = 4k^2, so q^2 = 2k^2 after dividing both sides by 2.
Now q^2 is also 2 times an integer, so q must be even as well.
Both p and q are even, so they share a common factor 2, contradicting the co-prime assumption from Step 1.
The assumption collapses into a logical disaster, so no such fraction exists.
examples.answer: sqrt(2) is irrational, exactly as Hippasus demonstrated around 400 BCE.

examples.title: Predicting a decimal without dividing
examples.problem: Without doing long division, decide whether 3/20 terminates or repeats, and find its decimal expansion.
steps: 3/20 is already in lowest terms, so inspect the denominator 20.
Prime factorise: 20 = 2^2 × 5; only 2s and 5s appear, so a terminating decimal is guaranteed.
Turn the denominator into a power of 10 by multiplying top and bottom by 5: 3/20 = 15/100.
Read off the decimal: 15/100 = 0.15.
examples.answer: 3/20 = 0.15, a terminating decimal, because 20 = 2^2 × 5 scales to the power of ten 100.

flowchart.title: How the World of Numbers unfolds

steps.label: Feel the need
steps.detail: Keeping count of cattle and days forces humans to count.

steps.label: Tally and match
steps.detail: Pebbles in a pot and notches on bone give the Natural Numbers.

steps.label: Welcome śhūnya
steps.detail: The Bakhśhālī bindu and Brahmagupta's 628 CE rules make zero a number.

steps.label: Step left of zero
steps.detail: Dhana and Ṛiṇa bring negative numbers, completing the Integers Z.

steps.label: Fill the spaces
steps.detail: Fractions and their inverses join the integers as Rationals Q.

steps.label: Meet sqrt(2)
steps.detail: Baudhāyana's fire altars reveal a diagonal no fraction can name.

steps.label: Prove the gap
steps.detail: Hippasus' proof by contradiction shows sqrt(2) is irrational.

steps.label: Unite the line
steps.detail: Rationals plus irrationals form the unbroken Real Numbers R.

steps.label: Read the decimals
steps.detail: Terminate or repeat marks the rationals; decimals tell the sets apart.
